FAST

TOKYO, Nov 17 : The dollar on Tuesday scaled a fresh 19-month peak against a basket of peers amid bets for more aggressive policy tightening by the US Federal Reserve following hot inflation data and hawkish central bank rhetoric. The US currency extended a 10-month high versus its Australian counterpart as a global selloff in AI stocks weighed on market sentiment, hurting the risk-sensitive Aussie. A sharper-than-expected acceleration in US consumer inflation last week triggered a run of five straight days of gains for the US dollar index, which carried into a sixth day on Tuesday with it rising to 103.66, the highest since April 2, 2025, when President Donald Trump rolled out his tariffs. The index measures the dollar against six rivals, including the euro, sterling and the Japanese yen. Traders now view a Fed interest-rate hike at the next meeting in December as a certainty, and they also lay around 4 per cent odds on a supersized half-point increase, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. A day earlier, those bets on an oversized hike were at nearly 12 per cent. A week earlier, there were 16 per cent odds for no change to policy.

Meanwhile, the tech selloff continued in Asia on Tuesday, with Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both firmly lower. A key test for AI sentiment - which has been rocked by the sudden departure of Nvidia's CEO, a Democratic sweep in US midterm elections and worries about a debt-fuelled AI infrastructure expansion - comes with the release of Nvidia earnings later in the day. The dollar has been supported by the AI boom as capital flowed into US markets. "Continued AI-related capital inflows and expectations of faster Fed tightening should support the USD," said CBA economist and currency strategist Carol Kong. "However, erratic US policymaking and a sharp correction in AI-related equities pose key downside risks to our bullish USD outlook." In terms of the Fed outlook, US retail sales data later in the day could offer further clues. The dollar edged to a fresh 18-month high of 0.84075 Swiss franc and rose slightly to 159.49 yen. Japan's currency has been hemmed in around 160 per dollar, which traders view as a potential trigger level for another round of intervention to support it. The euro slipped to a new 19-month low of $1.0985. Sterling fell to $1.3172. The Aussie dipped to $0.6725, the lowest since January.

Source: Reuters

Nov 17 : Oil prices fell on Tuesday as expectations of a supply surplus, fuelled by recovering Middle East exports, overshadowed concerns about continued attacks on tankers in the region. Brent crude futures were down 44 cents, or 0.5 per cent, at $92.00 a barrel at 0102 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures fell 44 cents, or 0.5 per cent, to $85.28. "Oil is recalibrating lower as the market increasingly accepts that supply has finally caught up with demand and may now be set to exceed it. That shift in the supply-demand balance is the main factor weighing on prices today," said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade. The International Energy Agency said on Friday that the world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite attacks on shipping.

Despite signs of improved supply, attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz have continued, maintaining uncertainty around one of the world's most important oil-export routes. "The geopolitical risk premium from the US-Iran conflict has not disappeared, but it is clearly taking a back seat for now," Waterer said. OPEC held an online meeting on Monday to discuss its review of members' maximum sustainable production capacity, a key exercise that will help determine OPEC+ output quotas for 2027 and beyond. The wider OPEC+ producer group, which includes allies led by Russia, is due to meet on November 29 to decide 2027 output policy. Elsewhere, stocks of crude oil in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 276.4 million barrels last week, the lowest level since August 1982, according to data from the Department of Energy. The recent drawdowns have been part of a US agreement to release 172 million barrels from the facility.

(Corrects to remove alert from story text) By Takaya Yamaguchi TOKYO, Nov 17 : Japan's Ministry of Finance will postpone the launch of a new type of floating-rate government bond as it reassess whether sufficient investor demand exists, two sources familiar with the matter said on Tuesday. The ministry had previously targeted issuance as early as January, but it has decided to defer setting a launch date until it determines whether demand for the securities would be sustainable, said the sources, who declined to be identified as the matter is private.

The move underscores how rapidly changing expectations for Bank of Japan interest rate hikes have altered conditions in the government bond market since the ministry began preparing the product in 2024. Unlike conventional fixed-rate bonds, floating-rate notes offer coupons that adjust with market interest rates, helping shield investors from losses when yields rise. The ministry originally saw such bonds as a way to maintain investor appetite for Japanese government debt as the BOJ moved away from years of ultra-loose monetary policy and began raising interest rates. However, bond markets have increasingly priced in future rate increases, diminishing the appeal of floating-rate notes as a hedge against rising yields, the sources said. The ministry had been considering issuing the new securities with a two-year maturity and sounding out whether investor demand would be strong enough to support regular issuance. It has since concluded that the plan merits further review, the sources said. The Ministry of Finance was not immediately available for comment. The decision will be reflected in Japan's fiscal 2027 government bond issuance plan, which is due at the end of this year following discussions with primary dealers and other market participants, including at a meeting scheduled for November 26, the sources said. The ministry will revisit the issuance plan during a mid-year review in June, the sources added. While Japan has previously issued 15-year floating-rate bonds, the proposed product would have been the country's first short-dated floating-rate government security, making it more directly linked to changes in monetary policy expectations.

Source: Reuters

Nov 17 : Former New Zealand under-23 coach Des Buckingham will take over the senior side from July next year and lead the All Whites through to the 2030 World Cup, New Zealand Football (NZF) said on Tuesday. The 41-year-old Englishman will also lead the under-23 side as they look to qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. "Des is a unique candidate for this role as he has a deep connection to New Zealand and the game here, as well as experience of coaching around the world at the highest levels with significant success across a wide range of environments," NZF boss Andrew Pragnell said in a statement. “This is huge for New Zealand Football and the future success of both NZF and the All Whites."

Buckingham will take up both roles after finishing his second season as head coach of Saudi Pro League club Al-Kholood. With Darren Bazeley signing off as All Whites coach with a 3-0 win over India in a friendly on Sunday, New Zealand will have an interim coach in charge for the March and June international windows. Buckingham coached New Zealand at the 2019 under-20 World Cup before being appointed under-23 coach. He has long coveted the senior job, having missed out to Danny Hay in 2019 and to Bazeley in 2023. Prior to his Saudi role, he returned to hometown club Oxford United in 2023 and led them to promotion into the Championship, ending a 25-year absence from the English second tier. He became the youngest coach in charge of an A-League team when appointed joint interim head coach of Wellington Phoenix in 2016 at the age of 31, sharing the role with Chris Greenacre.  Under Bazeley, New Zealand bowed out of the 2026 World Cup in North America in the group phase after defeats to Egypt and Belgium following a 2-2 draw with Iran. Buckingham will be charged with developing a playing group that can secure the nation a first match win at a World Cup and first appearance in the knockout phase at the 2030 tournament hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

Source: Reuters

Nov 16 : PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp said on Monday there are currently no plans to revive the "Returning Member Program" that earlier this year saw former LIV Golf player Brooks Koepka reincorporated into the US-based circuit. Rolapp, in his first media availability since LIV Golf announced on November 5 that it would begin winding down operations after a financing deal fell apart, said he is interested in doing what he can to make the PGA Tour better but is not rushing into any decisions regarding former players. "We have heard from our fans and we know that they want the best players playing together and we share that view," Rolapp said after a board meeting where the PGA Tour approved details for its new competitive structure set to debut in 2028. "I have said that from day one when I took the job, I am interested in doing whatever makes the PGA Tour better.

"That said, as we have a membership organization we have rules and as I shared before, they exist to ensure fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter and they will be enforced. "We engaged in thoughtful discussion on the topic of LIV players with both boards today. As far as we have read, bankruptcy proceedings are ongoing and the process is complex. I hope to have more to say in the beginning of the new year, but until that time, I will not speculate on the outcome or individual decisions players make." A number of leading golfers, such as former world number one Jon Rahm, announced their departures from LIV Golf after the rebel circuit filed for bankruptcy protection in September. Former LIV Golf players typically face a one-year suspension from the PGA Tour, a stretch that starts counting down from the date of their last unauthorised event on the rebel circuit. In January, Koepka took advantage of the limited-time offer after leaving LIV Golf last December. However, his return came at a cost, with the five-times major winner facing a five-year forfeiture of potential equity in the PGA Tour's Player Equity Program, representing an estimated $50-85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth. Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and former British Open champion Cameron Smith were also eligible to return under the same Returning Member Program that closed on February 2 after a three-week application window but decided to stick with LIV. They and others could now be forced to wait quite some time before seeing any form of "Returning Member Program" come their way. "There are no plans for that currently, no," Rolapp said when asked if a similar program would be offered in 2027.

Source: Reuters

CHICAGO, Nov 16 : United Airlines said on Monday it had resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures for about an hour, just days after a nationwide air traffic control outage caused widespread disruption to US airlines. The disruption, which ended around 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), highlighted how computer failures can ground flights even when aircraft and crews are ready to depart. There was no indication that United's outage was connected to Friday's Federal Aviation Administration shutdown, which caused the longest nationwide ground stop of departing flights since the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States. "We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," United said, adding flights already airborne and those operated by United Express had been unaffected throughout.

"There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," the airline said. An internal memo from United's pilots union, seen by Reuters, said a companywide web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. The memo said United had been unable to provide final aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates. Such information is essential for pilots to complete pre-departure calculations. In a subsequent memo, the union said United's systems were coming back online and directed pilots to check updated company communications. Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday's outage involved United's Unimatic system. Alaska Airlines also briefly halted departures nationwide in April 2024 after a problem with its weight-and-balance system. FLIGHT DISRUPTIONS As of 6:50 p.m. ET (2350 GMT), United had delayed 645 flights, or 20 per cent of its schedule, and canceled 25 on Monday, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. It was unclear how many of those disruptions were caused by Monday's technology issue, as airlines were still recovering from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop. United shares were down 2.5 per cent in after-hours trading. Some passengers reported on social media that their aircraft had returned to the gate after reaching the runway. The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The outage came as US air travel was largely returning to normal following Friday's nationwide ground stop, which lasted nearly five hours after a failure in the FAA's telecommunications network. More than 18,100 flights scheduled to depart US airports between Friday and Sunday were canceled or had not taken off within three hours of their scheduled departure times, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. Not all were necessarily affected by the FAA outage.

Source: Reuters

Nov 16 : JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Monday it experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug, adding that the issue may have affected other banks receiving its slowed transactions.  "JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence it is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a spokesperson for the bank said.  Customers can still access accounts and funds, and the bank is working hard to resolve the issue, the spokesperson added. "This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us."  The incident follows several other recent problems that have put users on edge, including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week, and Microsoft's global email outage, while last month crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack.

NEW YORK, Nov 16 : Rohit Chopra, secretary of the California Business and Consumer Services Agency, said greater accountability is needed from technology companies rolling out AI into the broader economy, and that his agency is already eyeing the possibility of taking those who fail to observe state rules to court. "There is no AI exception" to state legislation that mandates state licensing rules that govern everyone from doctors to bankers, Chopra told a Reuters Momentum AI Finance conference on Monday.  Chopra, the former head of the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, said he is concerned about the possibility that artificial intelligence companies may be acquiring and "weaponizing" consumer data, adding that he has little confidence federal regulators will be willing or able to step in and address problems via enforcement action. Specifically, he voiced unease about whether the Federal Reserve is assessing AI-related vulnerabilities.

"Or are they simply rooting all this on as cheerleaders? Because the economy, they have too many eggs in this basket," Chopra said, adding that he has "real worry" that any pullback or correction would end up jeopardizing the health of the overall economy. Self-regulation without enforcement makes it difficult to determine whether the technology companies' idea of self-regulation is adequate to address the potential risks of a new technology such as AI, he said. Chopra said state regulators are examining ways to collaborate around developing new rules and regulations governing the use of AI as it becomes increasingly ubiquitous. “We can’t just sit and watch,” he said, adding that states cannot simply rely on federal regulators to shoulder this task, nor can they leave it up to companies to self-regulate.  “We’re talking about breaking... the social contract” with American citizens, Chopra said.

BERLIN, Nov 16 : Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany hit four goals in 18 second-half minutes to thrash the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin on Monday and reach the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners. Germany, the Netherlands and Greece all finished on 11 points in Group A2 after substitute Giorgos Masouras scored in the 69th minute to give Greece a 1-0 win over Serbia at home. The Dutch advanced as runners-up and Greece finished third while Serbia ended the campaign without a point. It was the Netherlands' first defeat since Xavi Hernandez took charge in August. The Dutch had beaten Greece 7-0 three days earlier and needed a draw in Berlin to win the group.

Donyell Malen had a chance to put the visitors ahead but headed over from close range. Derry Scherhant hit the post at the other end before cutting in from the left in the 41st minute and firing into the top corner for his first international goal. The 24-year-old Freiburg winger grew up five minutes from the Olympiastadion, where he made his Bundesliga debut for Hertha Berlin. "What can I say? I don't think it could have gone any better. I couldn't even have dreamed of a better outcome. It's truly unbelievable. I had an incredible time out there and I'm just absolutely delighted," Scherhant said. Wirtz doubled the lead on the hour with a left-footed drive from outside the box that went in off the far post. Nico Schlotterbeck headed in Brajan Gruda's free kick five minutes later before Gruda set up Wirtz for a close-range finish in the 71st. "We always hope we can give the fans a lot of enjoyment. And we enjoyed it very, very much ourselves, especially in the second half," Wirtz said. Gruda turned in a rebound in the 77th minute after Scherhant struck the post. Germany's fifth goal secured top spot on head-to-head goal difference. The Dutch had last trailed by five goals in an international in 1959, when West Germany beat them 7-0 in Cologne. In St Gallen, Scotland lost 4-0 to already-promoted Switzerland in Group B1. Lewis Ferguson turned a cross into his own net in the 22nd minute before Winsley Boteli and Alvyn Sanches struck four minutes apart early in the second half. Substitute Zeki Amdouni added a late fourth.

Source: Reuters
